analysis.one_liner: Freezes cable TV rates at their March 1999 levels while the FCC studies rate increases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Commerce Committee's telecommunications subcommittee from April 1999 until that Congress ended in January 2001, with 10 cosponsors and no action after the referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Federal Communications Commission to bar cable companies from raising basic cable and cable programming rates above their March 1, 1999 levels, with the freeze staying in place until Congress acted after an FCC report. It also would have required the FCC to study how much cable rates rose from October 1992 to March 1999 and whether more competition could be created to hold rates down. The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who would be shielded from any increase in basic cable or cable programming rates above March 1999 levels for as long as the freeze stayed in effect. The required FCC study would also have given Congress and the public a documented account of why rates rose and what competition could do about it [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Freezes rates: within 10 days of enactment, the FCC would have had to order every cable operator to stop imposing or collecting any increase in basic cable or cable programming rates above the level in effect on March 1, 1999 [S2].

Forces a public accounting: the FCC would have had to investigate the extent and causes of rate increases from October 1992 through March 1999, assess whether competition had succeeded or failed in restraining rates, and report to Congress within six months on what could be done to extend competition and eliminate unjust or unreasonable rates [S3].

The freeze would not quietly expire: it would remain in effect until an Act of Congress passed after the FCC submitted its report, so rate relief would persist while Congress considered the findings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, whose revenue growth from rate increases would be halted for the duration of the moratorium; any cost of compliance and of the FCC inquiry would also fall on the industry and the agency [S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard rate freeze does nothing about the underlying problem the bill itself targets: limited competition. If cable operators' costs rose, a freeze could squeeze investment in networks and service quality rather than fix the market structure that lets rates climb [S3].

The moratorium is open-ended on the industry's side: it stays in effect until a future Act of Congress provides otherwise, which locks in 1999 rates without any automatic adjustment for inflation or cost changes [S3].

The bill addresses symptoms rather than structure. Even its own text concedes the real question is whether competition can be extended by FCC action, and a freeze alone would not create a second cable provider in any household's neighborhood [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers, the benefit is direct and immediate — a stop on rate hikes — while the costs fall on a concentrated industry. The honest weakness is design: freezing rates is a temporary shield, not a fix, and it does nothing to build the competition that would hold rates down permanently; the bill wisely pairs the freeze with a competition study, but the study alone would not lower anyone's bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and to its telecommunications subcommittee two weeks later, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Cable Rate Moratorium Act on March 25, 1999, with nine other original House sponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day, and on April 12, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S1].

Ten members cosponsored the bill (9 Democrats and 1 Independent), but the bill received no further action of any kind — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — for the rest of the 106th Congress [S4].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in subcommittee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators, who kept free rein to raise rates above their March 1999 levels, and the committee leaders who never had to schedule or answer for a vote on a rate freeze.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cable Rate Moratorium Act on March 25, 1999

for.name: 10 House cosponsors (9 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Hinchey, Frank, Thurman, Stark, Sanders, Weygand, Coyne, and Miller
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan-of-one bloc of support

against.name: House Committee on Commerce leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a vote after referring it to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection on April 12, 1999

against.name: Cable television industry
against.what_they_did: Would have lost the ability to raise basic and programming rates under the bill; no industry action on this bill appears in the congressional record

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no position was ever recorded; its support was almost entirely Democratic — 9 of 10 cosponsors were Democrats, with Independent Bernie Sanders the only non-Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have frozen their basic and programming rates at March 1, 1999 levels and subjected their pricing history to a public FCC investigation. Because the bill died in subcommittee, operators kept the ability to raise rates freely, which they had gained as the FCC's rate-regulation authority was being phased down.
